title: Japanese Enzyme Baths Find Fans at Home and Abroad
paragraphs: Imagine lying buried up to your neck in a warm bed of sawdust and rice bran. It may sound strange, but this treatment, known as an enzyme bath, is attracting a growing number of fans, both in Japan and overseas.

An enzyme bath is a type of heat therapy. Instead of water, people lie in a mixture of natural materials such as cypress sawdust, rice bran and herbs, which are mixed with microorganisms. As the microorganisms ferment the mixture, they naturally produce heat, which can reach between 40 and 70 degrees Celsius. Unlike in a sauna, the body is warmed gradually from the inside.

The treatment has been popular in Japan for decades. In recent years, new enzyme bath salons have continued to open. For example, in December 2025, a salon called Bran Room Koiwa began offering rice bran enzyme baths in Tokyo's Edogawa Ward, using only rice bran produced in Japan. According to the organization that supports such businesses, plans are underway to open 12 more locations across the country.

The trend has also spread abroad, particularly to South Korea, where enzyme baths have long been associated with middle-aged and older people. Now, however, they are becoming popular among young Koreans. According to data from Shinhan Card, people in their 20s and 30s made 47.5% of payments at enzyme bath businesses in the first quarter of 2026, up from 30.1% three years earlier. At one enzyme bath in Seoul, a single session costs 100,000 won, or about $65, but nearly 40 reservations are made on each day of the weekend, mostly by women in their 20s and 30s.

Celebrities have also helped make the treatment popular. In June 2026, Korean actress Oh Yeon-seo posted a video of herself buried up to her head in an enzyme bath. She explained that, unlike in a bath at home, the sweat seemed to come from deep inside her body.
Fans say that enzyme baths help them recover from fatigue, reduce swelling and improve their skin. Some businesses also claim that the treatment improves circulation and the immune system.
However, these claims mainly come from businesses and users, and there is little scientific evidence to support them.
